answer_1.quote: We study this question in the context of physicians deciding when to rely on Machine Translation (MT) in an emergency room ... The subset of selected English sentences were automatically translated into simplified Chinese by Google Translate ... The three bilingual physicians independently annotated each MT output along two dimensions: translation adequacy and clinical risk.
datasets: De-identified Emergency Department discharge instructions (28 sentences)
answer_1.outputs: Chinese translations of English discharge instruction sentences

answer_2.quote: While general translation quality is expected to be reasonably strong, on FLORES, the translation quality as measured by BLEU is 38.50 for the English‑Chinese (Simplified) devtest ... COMET‑QE achieves an accuracy of 66% and 73% on detecting adequate and clinically insignificant translations, respectively.

answer_4.quote: Three bilingual physicians independently annotated each MT output along two dimensions: translation adequacy and clinical risk. ... Physicians were asked to read a discharge instruction, see the Chinese translation, and decide whether they would give the translation to a patient ... also assess whether a monolingual Chinese patient would understand the discharge instruction using a five‑point Likert scale.
answer_4.guideline: Annotators judged translation adequacy (whether the Chinese translation accurately conveyed the meaning) and clinical risk (five‑level categorization from clinically insignificant to life‑threatening). Physicians then answered binary decision questions and confidence/understandability Likert scales.
